quote.text: Whosoever commands the sea commands the trade; whosoever commands the trade of the world commands the riches of the world, and consequently the world itself.
quote.author: Sir Walter Raleigh, A Discourse of the Invention of Ships (c. 1650)

stories.headline: The Cosmos on the Wrist, Now in Rose Gold
stories.dek: Ulysse Nardin's Blast Moonstruck folds five astronomical indications — a moonphase good for forty years, a worldtimer, the live positions of Sun and Moon, and the tides they pull — into a single 45mm case. This July it returns in 18-karat rose gold, twenty pieces, at just past a hundred thousand euros. A telescope you strap to your wrist, in the same issue a real one slips its launch (p16).

stories.headline: The Telescope That Didn't Launch, and the Comet That Was Caught
stories.dek: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was penciled for this weekend; instead it slipped to the end of August, fuelled and waiting on the pad. Meanwhile a Chinese orbiter at Mars did something rarer than a launch — it photographed an interstellar comet racing past the planet, only the third such visitor ever tracked through our solar system.

stories.headline: New Routes, a New Gulf Link, a Deeper Malaysia Map
stories.dek: The weekend's genuine deltas are about where you can now fly direct. Scoot has thickened its Malaysia network toward a hundred and thirty weekly flights, Oman Air has opened a Muscat link from Changi, and SIA has quietly turned Manchester and Hangzhou daily. Under the ground, the T5 tunnels are done and the RTS Link inches toward year-end. Delta only — a route already covered gets a line, not a re-explainer.

stories.headline: The War Finds the American Bases
stories.dek: For six months Washington fought Iran's reach and left its own soil alone. On the last day of July that line went too: Iranian drones on US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, two more tankers hit inside the Strait, and a barrel back near ninety dollars. Each capital now says the same thing in different words — that it can absorb more than the other can.

stories.headline: A Sixty-First Birthday, and a Bill to Read First
stories.dek: The island goes into its National Day weekend with the parade back at the Stadium next Sunday and a new drone show overhead — and, on the same kitchen table, July's 17 per cent power rise now landed and a second support package announced to soften it. The celebration and the cost of living arrive in the same envelope.

stories.headline: Nine More Sites, and a Two-Billion-Dollar Marquee
stories.dek: The buyer's market that arrived last quarter is not being rescued — it is being fed. Into a cooling resale market and a top-end-led private one, the second-half land programme keeps nine sites coming, led by a Bayshore plot analysts tip at up to two billion dollars. For an owner, the signal has not changed: supply, by design, for years.

stories.headline: Fifty Firms Ask Washington to Keep the Weights Open
stories.dek: The export fight has a new front, and it faces inward. An Nvidia- and Microsoft-led letter — signed inside a day by some fifty companies, from OpenAI and Google to Hugging Face and Mozilla, and pointedly not by Amazon or Anthropic — asks the administration to protect open-weight models rather than lock them down. The same machinery built to fence China out of American chips can, turned a few degrees, fence Americans in.

stories.headline: The Smallest Ring Wins the Wearable Argument
stories.dek: Oura's fifth ring is 40 per cent thinner than the fourth, runs six to nine days on a charge, and — now the summer reviews are in — is being called the best smart ring you can buy. For a reader already wearing an Oura and a Whoop, the useful question isn't whether it's good. It's whether one finger should be doing this much accounting.

stories.headline: The Release Grows Up Around the Edges
stories.dek: Last week 2026.8 was a beta with a cosmetic headline. This week it ships, and the substance is in the plumbing a Lutron household actually touches: dedicated infrared and radio-frequency panels, a rebuilt Zigbee stack, an activity timeline and a one-button "update everything." The catch is a quiet breaking change to the phone app — read it before you tap update.

stories.headline: The Second-Biggest Opening Ever, and the Coolest Reviews
stories.dek: The number No. 59 was still projecting has landed. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is estimated at around US$325 million domestic for the weekend — behind only Endgame — and close to US$925 million worldwide, on studio numbers that lock Monday. Audiences gave it a 98 that ties Marvel's best. The critics, uniquely of Tom Holland's five, ranked it last. The gap between those two facts is the whole picture.

stories.headline: The Screen-Time Panic Is Being Walked Back
stories.dek: The scary headline is easy to find: a 2026 study of fifty thousand children links four-plus hours a day of screens to sharply higher anxiety and depression. The quieter, more important story is that the American Academy of Pediatrics has just retired its decade-old hourly limits. The number was never the thing. What she watches, with whom, and what it displaces is.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Portfolio Lens
stories.headline: A Softer Dollar Meets a Firmer Barrel
stories.dek: No central bank moved this week, so the tape was written by two data points pulling opposite ways: a cooler June inflation print that knocked the dollar below 100, and a war that pushed Brent back toward ninety and the ten-year yield up to 4.75. The result is a crosscurrent, not a trend — US equities firm, Asia soft, and the reader's payrolls test still a week away. Market explanation, not advice.

stories.headline: The Apps Quietly Won — and One of Them Is Winning
stories.dek: A decade of hand-wringing about dating apps obscured the plainer fact: they are now simply how couples meet. About one in ten partnered adults — one in five under thirty — found their partner online, and among app-made marriages the field has consolidated hard around the app that sells intent over volume. The medium was never the problem. The volume was.

stories.headline: Zone 2 Isn't the Magic Bullet — It's the Floor
stories.dek: The longevity crowd spent a year worshipping easy "Zone 2" cardio; the 2026 reckoning is that it's necessary, not sufficient. A Sports Medicine review finds both easy volume and hard intervals raise the number that actually predicts how long you live — intervals faster, Zone 2 supplying the base you recover from. The prescription is both, plus the barbell. General information, not medical advice.

stories.headline: The On-Sale to Set an Alarm For
stories.dek: This weekend's alarm to set is the sumo: Aki Basho advance tickets open 8 August and the best seats vanish within hours. Behind it, an October stacked with arena nights — The Weeknd, the first F1 Sprint weekend, BIGBANG — and, before any of it, National Day itself.

stories.headline: The Narrows
stories.dek: Three of this issue's stories are the same story in different clothes: a strait, a chip, and a harbour. Each turns on the oldest lever in geopolitics — control of the narrow place through which everyone must pass. History is unusually clear about how that power ends.
